summary: # Marvelous Designer Tutorial: T-Shirt to Bunny Girl Costume (Part 2) ## Overview of Pressure Chart First, let's take a look at the overall distribution of the pressure chart when we press the Alt key. After the pressure chart is turned on, the grid color will change according to its strength. - **Red Area**: Tightest position - **Blue Area**: Widest position - **Green Area**: Also a tight position When making tight clothes, it is best to ensure that most areas are green or blue for a more visually appealing effect. ## Working on the Back Area Next, we will learn how to deal with the back area. Here, we use the **check tool**, which is located in the tool group of the internal drawing pattern. We can click and drag on the board to ensure that the widest position of the zero is near the waist. Upon releasing the mouse, we will see that two zero holes are dug on the waist. After that, we will use the **line tool** to sew the two sides of the zero hole together. This process saves part of the space on the board, making the whole design more three-dimensional and aligned with the human body's structure. ## Sewing and Simulation Then, we use the line tool to sew the two sides together and start the simulation. As you can see, there is more space on the board because the waist is dug out, which aligns well with the human body's structure. If any sharp corners appear, we can pull the rope a little longer to create a more natural shape. Since we intend to create a bunny girl costume, it may be necessary to cut more flatly at the back, so I will adjust the point of the rope down slightly. ## Adjusting Shrinkage Rate We can also use the ruler tool. Remember to set the shrinkage rate to negative to tighten a certain part of the board. This allows us to polish the area at the point of the rope. After opening the model, it may appear flat due to grid shrinkage. ## Checking for Issues Next, we can change the perspective to identify any problems with the dress. The first issue is the sleeve. The curve of the sleeve does not seem to relate well. For instance, when we view the back, it is clear that more adjustment is needed. If there is no movement in our hands, this part will actually be affected. We can use the **3D board tool** to draw a curve by clicking on the shoulder point and then pressing the Ctrl key to create a curve point. After loosening the Ctrl key, we can create a straight line point and double-click on the endpoint. ## Creating and Modifying Curves We will find a sharp corner at the bottom of the page. In the clothing design process, we aim to make the side of it a flat corner, so we need to pay attention when drawing this line. After that, we can use the built-in **multidirectional line tool** to draw a cut line along this reference line. Start by clicking the button and then pressing the Ctrl key to create a curve point. We also have the option to use the **edit line tool**. By selecting a line and right-clicking, we can choose to convert to an inner curve. If we select to change to the inner curve, the original 3D line will not appear, and this line will be converted to an inner curve. ## Adjusting Inner Curves Next, we zoom in to ensure that the inner curve point is positioned outside the board or above the outside board. The inner curve must contact the outside board to facilitate cutting. In the adjustment process, we can use the **edit curve point function** to smooth out the curve. After selecting this inner curve, we can choose to cut, allowing us to delete any excess boards. ## Managing Particle Diameter When closer to the camera or when a board is smaller, we may notice that the part outside the board line is still white. This area is simply the face of our grid, which appears larger than the outside board line due to a large particle diameter. Reducing the particle diameter will help this issue. After switching back to the black and white surface or the texture surface, we can operate on the back sleeve using the same method as before. ## Addressing Skirt Issues After simulating, we need to address other issues with the skirt. Firstly, the front appears overly large, resembling a sleeve, and has two obvious folds. Upon examining the transparent picture, we can see a small area at the bottom of the page that needs adjustment. To modify the curve line here, we need to press the Ctrl key to move along the original melody. While pressing the Ctrl key and using the mouse button, we can enter a specific number—I've tried 15 mm. ## Evaluating Curve Adjustments To judge if it is attached, we can pull the view slightly above the head. After modifying the curve line on this side, we can simulate again, and it should be closer to the human body's side. Now, we will deal with a prominent fold on the side. We can use a fake needle to click on both sides of this opening, combining the fold. We will see that the curve line is now relatively close to Hana's body curve. ## Adding Lines for Structure We can think of the method we created in the previous back piece. Here, we can also add a line to combine the two sides. To do this, we will choose the **add line tool**. In the middle position of these two fake needles, we will click to create a division point and then right-click to choose to add a line. After doing this, we can refer to the fake line created earlier and modify its width to 40 mm. After adjusting the fake line's width, we can delete the fake needle using the edit fake line tool. ## Final Adjustments Now, our breast line only opens to the widest point, which is understandable since the chest's position is the widest and requires the most material. This triangle can be adjusted to the most prominent point of the chest. After opening the pattern, the entire dress should now closely follow the curve of the human body. With the shape nearly complete, we can reduce the strength and conflict thickness of the chest. Next, we will evaluate the waist area. There is still some volume in the upper abdomen, while the back has less volume. We can use the **edit sheet tool** to reduce the front waist by 10 mm (1 cm). ## Adjusting Volume on the Waist It’s important to note that adjusting the waist significantly will not be effective, as it only affects the area near the waist. Thus, we need to find another method, which is to increase the length instead. Here, we will revert the large-distance adjustment we just demonstrated, returning to the position of about 10 mm. We have two creation methods: one is the same as before, clicking and dragging the mouse to adjust. The other method involves selecting the adjustment tool, placing the mouse at the bottom of the chest and at the same level as the side point of the waist, then clicking the left mouse button. This will prompt a specific creation value to appear. ## Finalizing Adjustments When creating a rope, we must ensure that both sides' widths are equal. For length, we can use the default value. We will first open a width of 10 mm on both sides, resulting in a total waist adjustment of 4 cm. After sewing the two sides together with the sewing tool, the overall structure should appear very close. If it's not close enough, we can widen the seam allowance. Using the adjustment tool, we can select the shape of the entire seam allowance. The midpoint can be used as a reference point for modifications, allowing us to adjust the width symmetrically on both sides. We may slightly widen it, but if the seam allowance is too wide, it can lead to protruding issues. Therefore, we can use the ruler for alignment or opt to make the seam allowance narrower. Given the side effects we plan to implement later, I will choose to maintain the seam allowance without modification.
